ranking.rationale: Prior inpatient utilization is one of the most robust predictors of readmission risk and should generalize across hospital/domain shifts better than demographics, payer, specialty, or sparse diagnosis/medication codes. It captures underlying disease burden and recent instability without relying on likely domain-identifying artifacts.

Prior emergency utilization is a strong, clinically meaningful predictor of readmission risk that should generalize across domains. It complements the already selected prior inpatient count by adding another stable facet of recent acute-care use, while avoiding more brittle hospital-process, demographic, payer, or specialty signals.

Length of stay is a strong, clinically meaningful indicator of illness severity and discharge complexity that should remain predictive of readmission across domains, while adding complementary stable signal beyond prior utilization counts.

Adds broad, clinically meaningful comorbidity burden beyond prior utilization and length-of-stay features. Total diagnoses is a stable severity signal for readmission risk and is less likely than payer, specialty, discharge, or demographic variables to encode domain-specific shortcuts.

Prior outpatient utilization adds strong, complementary signal to emergency/inpatient counts and length of stay by capturing chronic care intensity and healthcare engagement before the index encounter. It is semantically tied to readmission risk and should transfer better across domains than demographics, payer, specialty, or sparse diagnosis-code indicators.

Adds broad, encounter-level severity/intensity information that is clinically tied to readmission risk and should generalize across domains. It complements prior utilization features without relying on demographics, payer, specialty, or discharge artifacts that are more domain-specific or shortcut-prone.

Adds broad, clinically meaningful encounter-severity/treatment-intensity signal that complements prior utilization counts and length of stay. It is generally predictive of readmission risk across hospitals, while being less brittle than demographics, payer/race, specialty, or highly sparse diagnosis/medication-category indicators.

Discharge disposition adds strong, clinically meaningful signal about post-hospital care needs and illness severity beyond prior utilization, length of stay, and treatment intensity. It should remain broadly predictive of readmission risk across domains, while being less brittle than payer, specialty, race, or many sparse diagnosis/medication indicators.

Adds complementary encounter-intensity information beyond labs, medications, utilization history, length of stay, and discharge status. Procedure count is a clinically meaningful severity/treatment proxy that should remain predictive across domains, with less shortcut or domain-identifier risk than payer, specialty, race, or sparse diagnosis-code indicators.

Admission type adds broad, clinically meaningful context about acuity and planned vs emergency presentation that should remain predictive of readmission across domains. It complements prior utilization and length-of-stay features without relying on demographics, payer, specialty, or sparse diagnosis-code artifacts that are more domain-specific or brittle.

Diabetes medication use is a broad, clinically meaningful marker of diabetes severity and active management that should remain predictive across domains. It adds stable signal beyond utilization and length-of-stay features, while being less brittle than payer, specialty, race, or sparse diagnosis-code indicators and less artifact-prone than missingness-heavy lab-result categories.

Adds direct, clinically meaningful glycemic-severity information beyond utilization and treatment-intensity features already chosen. Elevated max serum glucose should remain predictive of readmission risk across domains, while being less brittle than payer, specialty, race, or missingness indicators and less redundant than more medication-status dummies.

HbA1c abnormality is a clinically meaningful, broadly stable marker of diabetes control and future readmission risk. It adds complementary physiologic severity information beyond utilization, length of stay, medication presence, and max glucose already selected, while being less domain-specific than payer, specialty, race, or sparse diagnosis-code indicators.

Insulin dose increase is a strong, semantically stable marker of poor glycemic control and treatment intensification, adding clinically meaningful signal beyond prior utilization, length of stay, diabetes medication presence, and lab summaries while avoiding brittle demographic or hospital-identity features.

Medication change during the encounter is a strong, semantically stable marker of clinical instability and treatment-response concerns that should generalize across domains. It adds useful signal beyond diabetesMed and insulin_Up by capturing whether any diabetes regimen was adjusted, while avoiding more domain-specific artifacts like payer, specialty, race, or sparse diagnosis-code indicators.

Age is a robust, semantically stable predictor of readmission risk across hospitals because it captures baseline frailty and chronic disease burden. Given the current set already covers utilization, acuity, LOS, and diabetes treatment intensity, adding an older-age indicator provides complementary patient-level risk without relying on brittle domain markers like payer, specialty, race, or missingness patterns.

A secondary diabetes diagnosis adds clinically meaningful comorbidity information not yet captured by utilization and treatment-intensity features. It should remain predictive across domains because diabetes burden and complication coding are semantically tied to readmission risk, while being less domain-specific than payer, race, specialty, or missingness indicators.

Adds complementary, clinically stable glycemic-control information beyond prior utilization and A1C features. A normal max serum glucose helps distinguish lower acute metabolic severity from the already selected high-glucose indicator, with better OOD robustness than demographics, payer, specialty, or sparse diagnosis/medication artifacts.

Adds complementary glycemic-control severity beyond the already selected A1Cresult_7 and glucose features. A markedly elevated HbA1c is a clinically stable predictor of poor diabetes control and future readmission risk, with less domain-specific shortcut risk than payer, race, specialty, or sparse medication indicators.

Older age remains a robust cross-domain risk factor for readmission and adds complementary signal beyond the already selected 60-70 bin, capturing the higher frailty/comorbidity burden of patients in their 70s without relying on demographic shortcuts like race or payer or brittle provider-specific artifacts.

Insulin dose decreases add clinically meaningful treatment-intensity information beyond insulin increases, diabetesMed, A1C, glucose, utilization, and length-of-stay features. This should remain semantically predictive of near-term readmission risk across domains, while being less brittle than payer, specialty, race, or missingness indicators and more informative than rare medication or diagnosis dummies.

Primary diagnosis of renal failure adds strong, clinically stable signal for readmission risk beyond utilization and diabetes-control features, capturing severe comorbidity burden without relying on demographics, payer, specialty, or missingness artifacts.

Adds a strong, clinically meaningful comorbidity signal: secondary diagnosis 584 indicates chronic kidney disease/renal failure, a robust driver of diabetes complications and readmission risk. It complements existing utilization and primary-diagnosis features without relying on demographics, payer, specialty, or missingness artifacts that are more domain-sensitive.

Adds a strong, clinically meaningful comorbidity signal—chronic kidney disease in a secondary diagnosis—that is plausibly stable across domains and complements existing utilization, severity, and diabetes-control features better than demographics, payer/specialty variables, missingness indicators, or redundant medication dummies.

Adds broad secondary-diagnosis burden/comorbidity information beyond the already selected specific diag_2 codes, likely improving stable readmission risk prediction while avoiding more brittle demographic, payer, specialty, or sparse medication artifacts.

Adds a strong, clinically meaningful comorbidity signal—chronic kidney disease/renal failure in an additional diagnosis slot—that should generalize across domains and complements existing utilization, severity, and primary/secondary diagnosis features without relying on demographics or hospital-specific artifacts.

Admitting physician specialty, especially internal medicine, adds broad clinical context about chronic-complex diabetes management and care pathway intensity beyond utilization, diagnoses, and meds already selected. It is more semantically tied to patient condition than payer/race/gender, and less brittle than rare medication indicators or missingness-heavy artifacts.

Heart failure as the primary diagnosis is a strong, clinically meaningful readmission risk signal that should generalize across domains. It adds complementary disease-severity information beyond utilization counts, length of stay, and the already selected renal/diabetes diagnosis codes, while being less likely than payer, race, gender, or specialty features to encode domain-specific shortcuts.

Heart failure as a secondary diagnosis adds strong, clinically stable readmission risk beyond utilization, LOS, and existing primary-diagnosis features. It is more semantically robust than payer/race/gender/specialty variables and less redundant than additional medication-state or missingness indicators.

Severe hyperglycemia adds robust clinical severity signal beyond prior utilization, LOS, A1C, and insulin-change features. The >300 glucose category is more actionable and stably predictive of near-term readmission risk than demographics, payer/race, specialty, missingness indicators, or sparse medication artifacts.

Nephrology specialty adds stable signal about chronic kidney disease/renal-complication management and readmission risk beyond the already selected utilization, labs, and diagnosis-code features. It is more semantically tied to patient condition than payer, race, gender, or missingness indicators, and less brittle than rare medication dummies.

Missingness of max glucose serum is often a strong, semantically meaningful marker of clinical concern and testing intensity, adding stable signal beyond observed abnormal glucose categories already selected. It is more broadly useful and OOD-robust than payer, race, gender, or specialty indicators, and less redundant than additional medication no/steady dummies.

Adds complementary signal to the already selected insulin change indicators: a steady insulin regimen captures active insulin treatment intensity without relying on brittle demographics or payer/site proxies, and should remain semantically predictive of readmission risk across domains.

Adds the remaining clinically meaningful HbA1c category, complementing the already selected abnormal A1C indicators. Normal A1C captures glycemic control and testing status in a way that should remain predictive across domains, with better stability than demographics, payer code, specialty, or sparse medication-specific artifacts.

Metformin use status adds broad, clinically meaningful diabetes-treatment intensity information that should generalize across domains. It is more stable and less domain-identifying than payer, race, gender, or specialty features, and more informative than rare-medication or missingness indicators given insulin, diabetesMed, A1C, glucose, utilization, and diagnosis features already selected.

Insulin use itself adds stable clinical signal beyond insulin dose-change categories already selected: being on no insulin versus any insulin reflects diabetes severity and treatment intensity, which should generalize across domains better than payer, race, gender, missingness, or specialty artifacts.

Missingness of the third diagnosis is a robust proxy for coding completeness and encounter complexity that can add signal beyond counts and specific diagnosis codes already selected, while being less domain-specific and less shortcut-prone than payer, race, gender, or specialty features.

Adds stable signal about active metformin treatment intensity beyond diabetesMed and metformin_No. Medication regimen details are clinically meaningful for readmission risk and generally more transportable than payer, race, gender, or missingness-heavy administrative features; it also offers better marginal value now than rare-drug indicators or additional diagnosis dummies already partly covered.

Metformin escalation adds stable clinical signal about diabetes severity and treatment intensification beyond existing utilization, labs, insulin, and baseline metformin indicators. It is more semantically tied to readmission risk than payer, race, gender, or specialty features, and less brittle than missingness-heavy or rare medication indicators.

Adds stable signal about active sulfonylurea treatment intensity beyond insulin/metformin and general medication-change features. This is clinically relevant to diabetes severity/management and should transfer better across domains than payer, race, gender, specialty-missingness, or sparse diagnosis/medication artifacts.

Secondary hypertension diagnosis adds robust comorbidity burden information beyond utilization, labs, and existing CHF/renal diagnosis codes. It is clinically linked to diabetes complications and readmission risk, and is more stable across domains than payer, race, gender, missingness, or specialty indicators.

Advanced age is a robust, semantically stable risk factor for readmission beyond the already selected 60-80 bins. The 80-90 group adds clinically meaningful nonlinearity in frailty/comorbidity burden and should generalize better than payer, race, gender, missingness, or specialty indicators, while offering more marginal value than rare medication flags already largely covered by insulin/metformin/change features.

Adds whether HbA1c was not measured, a clinically meaningful marker of diabetes monitoring intensity and care process that remains predictive across domains. It complements the already selected abnormal/normal HbA1c categories by capturing the missing-test group, with better expected stability than payer, race, gender, or specialty indicators and more marginal value than rare medication flags.

Age remains a semantically stable risk factor for readmission across hospitals and time, and the 50-60 band adds useful nonredundant age-gradient information beyond the already selected older age bins. It is more robust than payer, race, gender, specialty, missingness, or rare medication indicators, which are more likely to encode domain or practice-pattern artifacts.

Primary pneumonia diagnosis adds clinically meaningful readmission risk beyond utilization, labs, and existing CHF/renal diagnosis indicators. As a common acute condition, it is more likely to transfer across domains than payer, race, gender, or sparse medication artifacts, and it complements rather than duplicates the already selected diagnosis features.

Adds a robust comorbidity signal not yet covered: hypertension as an additional secondary diagnosis is clinically tied to diabetes severity and readmission risk, and should transfer better across domains than payer, race, gender, missingness, or rare medication indicators. Adds a common diabetes-treatment intensity signal not yet covered by insulin/metformin/glimepiride: stable glipizide use reflects outpatient glycemic management and disease severity, which should remain predictive across domains. It is more semantically stable than payer/race/gender or specialty features and less brittle than rare medication indicators.

Adds stable marginal signal about whether a common diabetes medication was not being used, complementing existing insulin/metformin/glimepiride/glipizide treatment features. This captures outpatient diabetes regimen intensity and disease management in a way that should generalize better than payer, race, gender, or specialty indicators, and is likely more informative than rare-drug or additional diagnosis dummies already partly covered by utilization and diagnosis-count features.

Adds complementary signal to the already selected medication-change indicators by explicitly capturing no medication change, a clinically meaningful and generally stable predictor of readmission risk. It is more robust across domains than payer, race, gender, or specialty features and likely offers broader marginal value than rare drug or highly specific diagnosis codes already partly covered.

Adds complementary comorbidity burden beyond primary/secondary diagnoses already chosen: heart failure as an additional secondary diagnosis is clinically tied to readmission risk and should remain predictive across domains. Missing medical specialty is common in this dataset and can stably reflect care setting/documentation intensity and case complexity beyond the specialties already selected. It adds broader signal than another rare medication or highly specific diagnosis code, while avoiding stronger shortcut risk from race or payer code.

Race can still add some stable signal through differences in diabetes complication burden and care patterns, giving the best remaining marginal predictive value despite needing a conservative prior.

Secondary coronary disease/ischemic heart disease diagnosis adds stable comorbidity severity signal beyond existing utilization, discharge, and heart-failure/hypertension codes. It adds complementary signal beyond utilization, labs, medications, and diagnoses already selected, while being more OOD-stable than payer code or many rare drug/specialty indicators.

Weight adds clinically meaningful diabetes-risk information that should transfer across domains, and selecting a concrete non-missing weight category complements the already chosen weight-missing indicator. Adds clinically meaningful body-size information beyond age, utilization, diagnoses, and missing-weight status already selected.
